APPROVAL OF MINUTES
  EL MONTE CITY COUNCIL ADJOURNED REGULAR MEETING

PARKING AUTHORITY; SUCCESSOR AGENCY TO THE FORMER EL MONTE COMMUNITY

TIME, SUCH OTHER BODIES OF THE CITY WHOSE MEMBERSHIP IS COMPOSED
EXCLUSIVELY OF THE MEMBERSHIP OF THE CITY COUNCIL

1.  CALL TO ORDER: 6:00 pm

4.  CLOSED SESSION (6:00 p.m. – 7:00 p.m.):

  The City Council and the various Authority Bodies whose membership is composed
  exclusively of the membership of the City Council (collectively, the “Council”) will attempt
  to address and complete all Closed Session business between 6:00 p.m. and 7:00 p.m.
  If the Council completes all Closed Session business prior to 7:00 p.m., the Council will
  take a short recess and commence all Open Session proceedings promptly at 7:00 p.m.
  In the event the City Council is unable to address or complete all agendized Closed
  Session items by 7:00 p.m., the Council will hear all such remaining items toward the
  end of the meeting, immediately following Council Communications. Should any member
  of the public wish to address the Council on any agendized Closed Session matter, the
  Council shall allow such person to address the Council on such matter prior to going into
  Closed Session, provided that all persons wishing to address the Council on an
  agendized Closed Session matter shall fill out a speaker card and be subject to a
  speaker’s time limit of 3 minutes per speaker and further provided that the Council shall
  be under no obligation to respond to or deliberate upon any specific questions or
  comments posed by a speaker or take action on any issue raised by a speaker beyond
  such action as the City Council may be lawfully authorized to take on an agendized
  Closed Session matter pursuant to the Brown Act (Govt. Code Section 54950 et seq.).

  Mayor Quintero invited members of the public to address the City Council on
  Closed Session Items 4.1 through 4.16.

  Mayor Quintero and the City Council recessed into Closed Session at
  approximately 6:07 pm. Councilmember Ancona joined the City Council in Closed
  Session at approximately 6:05 pm. Councilmember Ancona participated in all the
  Closed Session items discussed.

  Mayor Quintero and the City Council reconvened from Closed Session at
  approximately 7:10 pm.

8.  PUBLIC COMMENT REGARDING NON-AGENDIZED MATTERS:

  This time has been set aside for persons in the audience to make comments or inquiries
  on matters within the general subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council, the Housing
  Authority, the Financing Authority and/or the Water Authority (collectively, the “Council”)
  that are not listed on this agenda. Although no person is required to provide their
  name and address as a condition to attending a Council meeting, persons who wish to
  address the Council are asked to state their name and address. Each speaker will be
  limited to three (3) continuous minutes. Speakers may not lend any portion of their
  speaking time to other persons or borrow additional time from other persons.

  Except as otherwise provided under the Brown Act (Gov. Code Section 54950 et seq.),
  the Council may not deliberate or take action upon any matter not listed on this posted
  agenda but may order that any such matter be placed on the agenda for a subsequent
  meeting. The Council may also direct staff to investigate certain matters for
  consideration at a future meeting.

  All comments or queries presented by a speaker shall be addressed to the Council as a
  body and not to any specific member thereof. No questions shall be posed to any
  member of the Council except through the presiding official of the meeting, the Mayor
  and/or Chair. Members of the Council are under no obligation to respond to questions
  posed by speakers but may provide brief clarifying responses to any comment made or
  questions posed. The Council may not engage in any sort of prolonged discussion or
  deliberation with any speaker or group of speakers on matters that are not listed on this
  agenda.

  Enforcement of Decorum: The Chief of Police, or such member, or members of the
  Police Department as the Chief of Police may designate, shall serve as the Sergeant-at-
  Arms of any Council meeting. The Sergeant-at-Arms shall carry out all orders and
  instructions given by the presiding official for the purpose of maintaining order and
  decorum at the meeting. While members of the public are free to level criticism of City
  policies and the action(s) or proposed action(s) of the Council or its members, members
  of the public may not engage in behavior that is disruptive to the orderly conduct of the
  proceedings, including, but not limited to, conduct that prevents other members of the
  public from being heard when it is their opportunity to speak or which prevents members
  of the audience from hearing or seeing the proceedings. Members of the public may not
  threaten any person with physical harm or act in a manner that may reasonably be
  interpreted as an imminent threat of physical harm. All persons attending the meeting
  must adhere to the City’s policy barring harassment based upon a person’s race,
  religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical handicap, medical condition,
  marital status, gender, sexual orientation or age.

  David Lim – I live in El Monte as of three years ago. I bought a house and the problem

18.  COUNCIL COMMUNICATIONS/REPORTS:

  18A.  Mayor Quintero

  18A.1 Discussion Regarding Working Conditions for Transportation Network
  Companies.

  Mike Robinson – I have been driving for Lyft for 4 years thank you for letting us
  share our stories with you today. Outside of these Chambers you have been
  hearing from other drives about the way unfair gig companies affect our lives and
  the lives of our families. These stories reflect the reality of tens of thousands of
  drivers in California who are existing in or on the edge of poverty. As elected
  stewards of the City of El Monte I would like to ask you to consider how Uber and
  Lyft bad behavior affects everyone not just drivers and their families. These
  companies generate enormous amounts of revenue we are talking billions and
  empty hundreds of thousands of drivers. Who bares the cost of generating these
  billions, the public? All the infrastructures that Uber and Lyft use to make those
  billions is paid by us. We pay for infrastructure cost to maintain the roads that
  our cars drive on. We pay for public services like medical that many drivers
  depend on because Uber and Lyft fail to provide medical insurance for their
  workers. We pay for in our bodies because of emissions from the vehicles in the
  air that we breathe. While these companies avoid payroll taxes because they
  misclassify us as independent contractors. They are not just robbing drivers of
  paying us pennies on the dollar they are robbing the communities by avoiding to
  pay their fair share. Raising wages for drivers will go a long way from keeping
  some of that money here instead of sending it to the already rich Silicon Valley.
  Please help us keep Uber and Lyft accountable.

  Linda Valdivia – I am a mobile worker’s alliance member. I have been an Uber
  driver for the past three years. Tonight you have the opportunity to turn the page
  not just in El Monte but across California and in our whole Country. For years we
  the drivers have spoken out about Uber and Lyft’s exploitation. Despite Uber and
  Lyft paying us poverty wages the companies keep getting more and more money
  with their investments and they keep getting richer. Some City mayors have even
  participated in the initial public offering ceremonies but not here. I am proud to
  know that El Monte is listening to our concerns. We are not asking for the moon
  what we are asking for is a wage that we can live on. We are asking for a wage
  that can cover our expenses with. Right now Uber and Lyft take home all the
  profit when we bring all the capital. Imagine if your five fire companies were
  required to use their own fire trucks and fill them up with their own water and pay
  for the gas and on top of that they never get a day off. This is the reality that we
  share as rideshare drivers. We need champions we need public officials like you
  we need to say enough is enough. By taking a stand you can make a difference
  you can end the economic abuse you actions can inspire all the leaders to also
  do the right thing. I hope you take this opportunity and inspire other cities to
  follow El Monte.

  Leonardo Diaz – I am proud to be a mobile worker’s alliance member. I have
  been driving for Uber and Lyft for four years and a half and I want to say that
  when people we don’t have too much money we are submissive and humble.
  But this is the story with Uber and Lyft they started their businesses giving good
  promotions to motivate us. Today they are humiliating our partners and are
  deactivating some accounts for little reason or no reasons. During this time I
  have seen these companies getting worse by paying us less and less but you
  know better than I what keeps going up the cost of living and the expenses that
  keep me on the road has gotten so bad. Most of the time we make less than
  minimum wage before driving expenses. Even after driving more than 40 hours
  a week we struggle to make ends meet. But you know who doesn’t struggle
  Uber and Lyft they are worth millions of dollars and they keep getting rich every
  day because of me and my partners on the road. It is unfair and unsustainable
  for us drivers to keep working this way I feel like I can never see my family
  because I am always working. I thank you for listening to our story and I
  encourage you to establish $30 an hour living wage here in El Monte. El Monte
  is going to be the main center to start and then over California and other States.
  A $30 an hour living wage will do so much for this community this is a working

  9
  City Council Adjourned Meeting Minutes of August 7, 2019

class community many workers are already working multiple jobs man y are
driving 20 or more miles to go to get those jobs. The establishment of $30 an
hour for rideshare workers will allow them to stay closer to home that means
staying closer to our families. This wage will give us true flexibility not the fake
flexibility that Uber and Lyft they say they offer. We should not have to choose
between driving more hours to survive or spending quality time with our families.
Again, thank you for listening to us.

Yadira Orozco – Good evening Mayor and City Council my name is Yadira
Orozco and I am a driver for Uber and Lyft I am a resident of El Monte and have
been living here for 26 years with my three children. I have driven for Uber and
Lyft for about a year and I have seen how the companies keep cutting our pay
every day they want to pay us less I drive from Monday through Saturday on
average 12 to 16 hours a day. If I miss a day because I don’t feel well I don’t earn
an income. I work a lot of hours and I have very little show for it why because
Uber and Lyft continuously slash our pay and we the drivers are shouldering the
costs. We pay for the gas, the tires, and the vehicle maintenance it is an
injustice and it affects everyone in this community. Let’s be clear the majority of
Uber and Lyft drivers are Latino and in this City the largest demographic is also
Latino what happens to us also impacts this community if you raise the wage to
$30 an hour in this City you will be helping thousands of families like my own.
Please take this challenge as an opportunity to help us workers and immigrants
that form a great part of El Monte community please don’t let this opportunity of
raising the wage to $30 an hour go to waste it would go a long way to bring a just
and fair treatment for us as workers. Thank you.

Reynaldo Blandon – I am here to express my concern and thank you guys for
taking us and for helping us and supporting us. One thing that Uber and Lyft are
forgetting is that all of us here we have been saving thousands of lives for so
many years. I am referring to drunk individuals. They are pretending, they keep
wasting money acting like NASA doing cars running by themselves that isn’t
going to happen because they are not going to save lives. We have been driving
during the nights and we have seen city workers putting cones on the freeways,
closing the street and meanwhile we follow GPS and it tells us to go and go and
go and that may cause an accident by us as a human being we can catch it a car
driving itself is going to kill people. Meanwhile they are wasting money because
they have a plan for 2020 building drones they have money but they keep
wasting their time doing drones having plans for making cars that drive by
themselves it is not going to help. I just wanted to let you know that we are
angels on the road 24/7.

Wendy Knight – I am a research and policy analyst SEIU Local 721. Drivers are
here tonight to demand a $30 an hour living wage or a $15 an hour in take home
wages and $15 to cover the costs of doing rideshare business which makes
perfect sense in a City with the largest bus terminal west of Chicago where a
large number of first and last mile rides originate. The City should capture some
of the revenue from those rides by ensuring that drivers here make a living wage
allowing them to spend here and contribute to the local economy. Absent specific
data from Uber and Lyft to 2018 study by the Economic Policy Institute found that
after factoring in operating expenses and nominal employer paid benefits the
average Uber and Lyft driver earns $9.21 per hour. Our own survey of more than
200 drivers found that seventy five percent of them in the L.A. Area make less
than $15 before their expenses. In order to ensure that the drivers are
compensated appropriately a $30 standard would allow them to cover a portion
of the hundreds sometimes thousands of dollars that they pay out of pocket for
costs borne simply operating their vehicles. Experts in New York City determined
that the average driver incurred $20,295 per year in operating expenses alone.
The average driver works for at least 30 hours per week so that amounts to an
accrual rate of $13 just for expenses without accounting for benefits typically
provided by an employer such as unemployment insurance, workers comp and
health insurance. A living wage ordinance that captures the $15 base salary
wage and a $15 allowance for operating expenses and other benefits will also
serve to relief the public safety net. Our survey revealed that fifty two percent of
drivers rely on public assistance programs like Medical, CalFresh, My Health LA
or a housing assistance program. Implementing a $30 an hour for a living wage
ordinance for TNC drivers will go a long way towards lifting families out of poverty
and helping to set standards across the Country establishing this wage is fully
within your prevue as a City Council. You have the authority, you have proof of

  10
   City Council Adjourned Meeting Minutes of August 7, 2019

concept and subject matter experts that you can consult and as you can see by
the number of driver turnout here tonight you have the demand to make a $30 an
